chunks: Rules of thumb for writing ISRs. The question: What are some rules of thumb when implementing ISRs?
An ISR is the short function the hardware runs when an interrupt happens. While it runs, it holds up other work, so a few habits keep it harmless.
Keep it very short, clear the interrupt flag, never wait for anything, and hand the real work to the main code. Each rule prevents one specific failure.
Think of a receptionist. When a visitor arrives, the receptionist notes the name, presses the buzzer, and passes the visitor on.
A long conversation at the desk would leave everyone else standing in the lobby.
The picture breaks down in one place: the receptionist can write down many visitors, but a peripheral's flag only records that something happened, so a slow ISR can lose arrivals.
Load grows linearly with the control ISR time, reaching 100% when the ISR fills the whole 50 microseconds period.
A 12 microseconds ISR gives about 28% total, which is comfortable; lengthening it to 25 microseconds already hits 50% total.
ISR: ("What an ISR is"): the handler function that the hardware runs for an interrupt.
Flag: a bit in the peripheral (the hardware block, such as the serial port) that says "I need service". Clear it, or the ISR runs again at once.
Blocking: waiting for something else to happen, such as a delay or a lock. Deferred work: the ISR leaves a note (a flag or a queue) and the main code does the heavy part later.
A UART (a serial port) at 115,200 bits per second delivers a byte about every 87 microseconds. A good ISR reads the byte, puts it in a buffer, and sets a flag.
That takes about 2 microseconds, roughly 2. 3% of the processor's time. A bad ISR parses a whole command and prints a reply, taking 500 microseconds.
About five more bytes arrive meanwhile (500 / 87 is about 5. 7), and without a hardware buffer they are lost. That is the whole idea.
"Keep ISRs short, a few microseconds, since they delay everything else. Clear the flag correctly and only what you handled.
Never block or call printf, malloc or anything slow or non-reentrant. Make shared variables volatile and update them atomically, ideally one writer per variable or a ring buffer.
Defer the real work to main or a task by setting a flag or posting to a queue.
Assign priorities by deadline, budget stack for nesting, and measure the worst-case ISR time on a scope."
